description: Solo participant from Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, taking on the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. I'm interested in lunar exploration and in turning complex NASA data into simple, clear tools. Skills: Python, data analysis, data visualization, web development. My focus: scientific accuracy and an interface anyone can understand in seconds.
summary: Lunar Window Finder is a one-screen web tool that shows whether a lunar lander will have sunlight for its solar panels and a direct line of sight to Earth at a chosen site on chosen dates. At the Moon’s south pole the Sun never rises more than about 1.5° above a flat horizon, so mountains decide everything. We compute the real horizon of each site from NASA LOLA terrain and combine it with Sun and Earth positions from NASA JPL Horizons for every hour of 2027–2028. The tool gives a one-sentence GO / NO-GO verdict against a mission rule (for example, at most 50 hours of darkness) and, if the answer is NO-GO, finds the nearest landing date that works: the “launch slipped” case from the challenge. It covers the nine Artemis III candidate regions, their best-lit spots, 13 real missions and any point you click near the pole. Results match NASA’s illumination map within 1.6 percentage points on average. It matters because a move of a few kilometres can change sunlight from 2% to 64% of the time, and planners, teachers and the public can now see that in seconds. New on day 2: it also checks landing safety, the ground slope from the same NASA map against the 5 deg limit of NASA's crew lander. details:
Live tool (no login needed): https://imranio07.github.io/lunar-window-finder/

WHAT IT DOES

- Pick a landing site, a landing date and hour (any hour of 2027-2028), a mission length, a panel height (2 m lander deck or 10 m mast) and a mission rule.

- Read the verdict in one sentence, with six key numbers: Sun elevation at touchdown, time until sunset, solar availability, longest darkness, Earth line of sight, longest communication blackout. Each number is also shown for a horizon 0.1 degrees higher and lower, so the user sees how sure the result is.

- See the sky with the real terrain silhouette and the paths of the Sun and Earth, and a timeline of both above the local horizon, including eclipses (Earth passing in front of the Sun).

- Compare everything at once in the feasibility calendar: every site against every landing day of 2027-2028, coloured GO / NO-GO for the chosen rule. A table ranks all sites for the chosen date.

- Pick your own point: click anywhere on a shaded-relief map of the south pole, or type any lunar coordinates. The page computes the horizon of that point in the browser.

- Explore a sunlight map of each Artemis III candidate region (about 400 points per region) and jump to its best-lit spot.

- Open 13 real missions (Apollo 11 to 17, IM-1, IM-2, Chandrayaan-3, Chang'e 4 and 6, SLIM, Blue Ghost 1) at their real landing moment.

- Get a rough power check: energy per square metre of panel, panel area, battery for the longest night.

- For teachers and the public: "Bishkek vs the Moon" compares the Sun's path over our city with its path at the landing site.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Sun and Earth: NASA JPL Horizons API, apparent azimuth and elevation for a point on the lunar surface (hourly for 2027-2028, every 10 minutes around real landings, every 6 hours over 18.6 years for the checks). Horizons already includes the Moon's orbit and libration.

2. Terrain horizon: NASA LOLA south-pole height map at 80 m per pixel. From each site we cast 720 rays (every 0.5 degrees) out to 150 km and keep the highest terrain angle, corrected for the curve of the Moon: angle = atan((h - h0 - d*d/(2*R)) / d). The Moon has no air, so there is no refraction.

3. Visibility: the share of the Sun's disk (0.53 degrees wide) and Earth's disk (1.9 degrees wide) above the local horizon at each time step, and the share of the Sun covered by Earth during eclipses.

4. Region scan: the USGS outlines of the nine Artemis III regions are covered with a grid; the best-lit point of each region is then recomputed in full.

5. One static web page (HTML and JavaScript, no server, no external libraries) draws everything and repeats the same formulas in the browser, so every control responds at once. For a clicked point it reads a 240 m version of the LOLA map and casts the same 720 rays itself; its result matches the Python pipeline within 0.001 degrees.

WHAT WE FOUND

- Where you land inside a region matters more than which region you choose. In Slater Plain the centre of the region gets sunlight 2% of the time in 2027-2028; a spot 4.5 km away gets 64%. In Mons Mouton: 22% at the centre, 53% at a spot 5.7 km away.

- The best-lit spot of de Gerlache Rim 2 has the shortest "longest night" of all nine regions: 160 hours (6.7 days), against 13 to 19 days elsewhere.

- A 10 m mast instead of a 2 m deck can double the sunlight where a small bump stands within a few hundred metres (one check point: 11% to 23%).

- Chang'e 4 and Chang'e 6 see Earth about 40 degrees below the horizon: the tool shows at once why they needed a relay satellite.

HOW WE KNOW IT IS RIGHT

- NASA's average illumination map (PGDA, Mazarico et al. 2011, 18.6 years): at 20 check points between 85.5 degrees South and the pole our result differs by 1.6 percentage points on average (largest 3.3, correlation 0.995).

- NASA's Earth visibility map: 0.6 percentage points on average (correlation 0.997); 17 of 20 points agree to 0.1.

- Apollo landings (Apollo Lunar Surface Journal): Sun position within 0.05 degrees, Earth within 0.35 degrees, for all six landings.

- A real mission: for Blue Ghost Mission 1 the tool gives 348 hours from touchdown to sunset; Firefly Aerospace reported 346 hours of daylight operations. The tool also finds, on its own, the eclipse of 14 March 2025 that the lander filmed from the surface.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

A mission planner can compare sites and dates in seconds and get a new landing date at once when a launch slips. A teacher or student can see why the lunar south pole is so hard. The tool is free, runs in any browser with no install and no server, and its code and method are open, so anyone can re-run it for new sites.

WHAT IS CREATIVE

- It turns positions and maps into a decision: GO / NO-GO for a mission rule, plus the nearest landing date that works.

- It looks inside each Artemis III region instead of treating a region as one point, and shows how a few kilometres change everything.

- The browser itself computes the horizon of any clicked point: the terrain is packed into an ordinary image file.

- It checks itself against four independent references, including a real eclipse and a real mission.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Panel height (2 m deck or 10 m mast), the uncertainty of the horizon (every number is repeated for plus or minus 0.1 degrees), eclipses, libration (through Horizons), the curve of the Moon, the missing atmosphere, and the resolution and the edge of the height map.

LIMITS WE STATE OPENLY

Sunlight in view is not electric power, and Earth in view is not a radio link: panel angle, dust, temperature, antennas and ground stations are not modelled. The 80 m height map smooths ridges closer than about 1 km and ends at 80 degrees South, so for sites north of about 85 degrees South some far terrain is not counted. The click-any-point mode is a quick look on a 240 m map: at 19 sites computed both ways it differs from the full calculation by 2.4 percentage points of sunlight on average, and by up to 15 next to a close ridge. The best-lit spots are our result, not NASA's selection.

TOOLS

Python (NumPy, Rasterio, Requests), JavaScript, HTML and CSS, Git, GitHub Pages. An AI assistant (Claude by Anthropic) helped write the code, the texts, the demo video and the slides; the author ran every step and checked the results against the NASA references above. No numbers or results were generated by AI.

LANDING SAFETY: GROUND SLOPE (added on day 2)

Sunlight is not enough: a lander also needs gentle ground. IM-2 Athena (March 2025) ended on its side in a crater. The tool now measures the ground slope from the same NASA LOLA 80 m map (height difference between points 80 m on either side) at every site and at every point of the region maps.

- New rule "Max ground slope": 5 deg (the limit for NASA's crew lander used in Artemis III site studies), 10 deg or 15 deg. A site steeper than the limit is NO-GO on every date, and the tool says that no landing date fixes it.

- Slope map of each Artemis III region, with the best-lit point that is also gentle enough marked "safe".

- Slope column in the comparison table; steep sites are marked in the calendar.

What we found: with the 5 deg limit, 4 of the 9 best-lit spots are too steep (Peak near Cabeus B, Haworth, Mons Mouton Plateau, Nobile Rim 2). In Peak near Cabeus B only 5 of 400 scan points are under 5 deg. In Slater Plain 26% of the points are, and its best-lit spot (64% sunlight) slopes only 2.9 deg.

Limit: an 80 m map smooths small bumps, so the real slope under a lander's feet can be steeper. This is a first screening; certifying a spot needs 5 m maps. Where the tool has no terrain map, there is no slope value and the rule is not checked.

Reference for the 5 deg limit: arXiv:2406.19863, https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.19863
